text: A randomised trial evaluated serum K for iron-deficiency anaemia in pregnant women in the second trimester. 276 participants were enrolled for 8 weeks. The primary result was a rise in haemoglobin of 1.4 g/dL by week 8; a secondary finding was a reduction in reported fatigue on a standard questionnaire. In terms of comparison, serum K raised haemoglobin faster than oral supplementation. No serious adverse events were attributed to the infusion. The effect was largest in women with the lowest baseline haemoglobin. Cost per course was noted as a barrier to routine use. A pre-specified subgroup of interest was women who could not tolerate oral iron, who were few in number but showed a similar direction of effect. Over time: in 2018, the trial reported a 1.4 g/dL haemoglobin rise; in 2022, a pooled analysis of three trials put the rise at 1.1 g/dL. The authors concluded that serum K corrects anaemia in pregnancy quickly, which matters most when oral iron is not an option.
